English · [Français](how-studium-works.fr.md)

# How Studium works

Studium plays a lesson as a series of scenes tied to an explicit graph of concepts. Each answer is graded by whoever holds its key, only graded evidence moves the learner's mastery, and spaced reviews bring a concept back when recall fades. This page shows the whole loop; each part has its own page.

## The lesson bundle

A lesson is one file, `lesson.json`, called a *lesson bundle*. It holds:

- metadata: title, language, and who drafted the lesson (`metadata.authoring`); - the concepts and the Learning Workflow Graph that links them; - the scenes, in order, each tied to one or more concepts; - adaptation rules, and optionally *universes* (a baseline and a more scaffolded remedial variant); - `validated_by`, the name `approve` wrote, or a `DRAFT` / `SELF-STUDY` placeholder. Whether the lesson is validated is read from its approval record (`approval.json`), never from this text.

The format is described in the [lesson bundle reference](../reference/lesson-bundle.md). Check any bundle with:

```bash node tools/bundle_lint.mjs path/to/lesson.json ```

A lesson can come from four places:

| Origin | How it is made | Drafted by | Teacher-validated | |---|---|---|---| | Teacher course | `tools/experience_packet.py` (`passages`, `prepare`, `check`, `bundle`), then `approve` | teacher | yes, once approved | | Lesson from your sources, in a conversation | MCP tools `get_authoring_guide`, `prepare_sources`, `create_lesson` | agent | no | | Self-study from your references | `experience_packet.py bundle --self-study` | learner | no | | Learner contribution | proposed by a learner, reviewed and released by a teacher | learner | yes, once released |

See [Learn with your assistant](../learn/learn-with-your-assistant.md) and [Author a lesson](../teach/author-a-lesson.md).

## Scenes

A scene is one step of the lesson: an introduction, a concept, a question, a text to audit, a reproduction to run. There are 13 scene types. Each expects a typed answer: a choice, a text, a confidence level or a run result are not interchangeable. Each type belongs to a *key class* that says who can grade it. See [Scene types](scene-types.md).

The learner never sees a key before answering, on any surface. The reference answer and the cited source passages of a graded scene are released after the answer, when the learner leaves the scene for good.

## The graph

The Learning Workflow Graph (LWG) has two kinds of nodes, *concepts* and *tasks*, and typed edges: `prerequisite_for`, `part_of`, `decomposes_into`, `assesses`, `aligns_with`. The graph is part of the bundle, so a teacher can read and correct it.

A concept becomes available once each of its direct prerequisites reaches a mastery of 0.8 (0.6 in a universe marked `lenient`). When a prerequisite is missing, the session can route the learner to it first and then return. The graph is visible in the VS Code pane and through `get_workflow_graph`.

## Mastery and adaptation

For each concept Studium keeps a Beta estimate of mastery, fed only by answers that were actually graded: a marked choice, a verdict deck scored against its key, or a model judge. A keyword match never counts. Hints reduce the credit of a correct answer. Mastery is certified only after at least three graded attempts and a posterior of 0.8 or more.

After each answer, the bundle's adaptation rules and the graph decide what comes next: replay after repeated errors, skip a concept already mastered, show a calibration panel when declared confidence and measured mastery diverge, or detour to a prerequisite. `explain_last_adaptation` returns the rule that fired and its *modulator*, the label of its pedagogical intent. See [Learner model](learner-model.md) and [Modulators](modulators.md).

## Reviews over days

Each graded answer, and each self-rating, updates an FSRS memory per concept: how stable the memory is and how likely the learner is to recall it now. `get_study_plan` lists what is due across all lessons, and `start_review_session` plays it. A self-rating schedules reviews but never moves mastery. See [Review over time](../learn/review-over-time.md).

## Who wrote the key

Every lesson start and every presentation carries an `authoring` block: who drafted the lesson, whether a teacher validated it, whether a judge model is configured, an approval record if one exists, and a notice for lessons no teacher wrote. A lesson an assistant drafted from your sources says so on its first screen. See [Honesty and provenance](honesty-and-provenance.md).

## Surfaces

The same session contract is served to every surface.

| Surface | Status | |---|---| | Any MCP harness (Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, OpenCode, Cursor), and the file channel for harnesses without MCP | supported | | VS Code extension: lesson pane and chat participant | supported | | `lesson-server` (HTTP, answer keys redacted), teacher dashboard, Observatory | maintained | | Tauri student app (`apps/student-runtime`) | frozen | | `author-web` | legacy |

Studium keeps the lesson, the keys, the progression and the run protocol. The harness owns its tools, its model and its execution environment: it relays scenes and runs reproductions, the learner answers, and the teacher decides what is released. See [Harnesses](../start/harnesses.md), [VS Code](../start/vscode.md) and [Architecture](../develop/architecture.md).

# Honesty and provenance

Studium tells the learner who wrote each answer key, whether anything actually assessed their answer, and whether a teacher validated the lesson. This page explains how: key classes, the judge, self-rating, the notices, source quotes, the approval record, and the rule that no content reaches students without a teacher.

## What every lesson declares

`start_lesson_session`, `get_operator_context` (and so the file channel's `task.md`) and each presentation carry an `authoring` block. The VS Code pane shows its notice as a banner.

| Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `mode` | `teacher` (default) or `self_study` | | `author_is_learner` | the learner wrote the lesson | | `validated` | true only when an approval record matches this exact `lesson.json`; never for a self-study lesson; `validated_by` text never sets it | | `judge` | a judge model is configured on this server | | `notice` | the text shown to the learner for a self-study lesson; null for a teacher lesson | | `approval` | whether an approval record exists (`approval.json` next to the lesson, or the `approval.json` member of a lesson `.zip`), whether it matches this exact `lesson.json`, and its `reviewer` |

Who drafted the lesson comes from `metadata.authoring.drafted_by` (`teacher`, `learner` or `agent`); a self-study bundle without it reads as drafted by the learner.

The approval record is the only source of the validated status. Every surface (the first screen of the conversation, the panes, `list_lessons`, the concept map page) tells three states apart:

| State | When | What the learner reads | |---|---|---| | Approved | a record matches the sha256 of the loaded `lesson.json` | « Leçon validée par <reviewer> » / "Lesson validated by <reviewer>", the name taken from the record | | Changed since approval | a record exists and does not match | a first-screen notice that the lesson changed after the teacher approved it | | No record | no record, or a malformed or foreign one | « Aucune approbation enregistrée pour cette leçon. » / "No approval is recorded for this lesson." |

A learner's contribution a teacher reviews (`mode: "teacher"`, `drafted_by: "learner"`) reads as proposed by a classmate (« Leçon proposée par une personne de la classe, validée par <reviewer>. » / "Lesson contributed by a classmate, validated by <reviewer>.", or the classmate sentence followed by the no-record sentence), and its key as written by a classmate, never as the reader's own. A self-study lesson keeps its own notice and never reads as validated. A name typed into `validated_by` by hand, without a record, shows nowhere as a validation.

## Key classes

Every scene type belongs to one of four key classes ([`key-class.ts`](../../packages/lesson-session-host/src/key-class.ts)). `experience_packet.py check` prints them on its `Key classes:` line and the linter repeats them.

| Class | Scene types | Who holds the key | In a self-study lesson | |---|---|---|---| | `ungraded` | `intro`, `concept`, `meta_checkpoint` | nobody | nothing is graded | | `author_keyed` | `quiz`, `spot_the_flaw` | the author of the lesson | open book when the author is the learner; unchecked when an agent drafted it | | `production` | `explain_back`, `comparison`, `summary_audit`, `prompt_practice`, `communication_sim`, `discussion`, `ai_critique` | a judge model, if configured | without a judge, the reference is shown and nothing is assessed | | `externally_grounded` | `reproduction` | an executed run, checked against its manifest | the only key no author wrote |

## The judge

A judge is a model the server reaches through `LITELLM_BASE_URL`. `get_server_info` reports `model_backend: configured` or `none`. Only an evaluation whose source is the model certifies a free-text answer; a score of 0.6 or more counts as correct.

Studium no longer grades free text by keywords. Matching authored cue words anywhere in an answer measures vocabulary, not understanding: measured against a teacher on a real lesson, it inverted 11 answers out of 12. Without a judge, the feedback shows the reference to compare with and states no count.

## Who assessed an answer

Every verdict says who assessed the answer in `assessed_by`: `key` (the author's key, for a quiz or a verdict deck), `judge` (the judge model) or `none` (nobody: an unjudged written answer, an acknowledgement). `graded` only means that an answer was submitted. The text shown to the learner marks ✓ only when `correct` is true and ✗ only when it is false; an answer nobody assessed is shown as recorded.

After the answer, a verdict carries its reference as data, labelled by `reference_kind`: the key points an answer should cover, the planted flaws, the claims a critique should challenge, or `correct_choice`, the text of the right choice when a quiz was answered wrong ("The right answer"). Like the cited passages, the reference is released only when the learner leaves the scene for good; a retry of the same item keeps it back.

## Self-rating

After a free-text answer no judge assessed, the learner rates their recall: again, hard, good or easy. The rating schedules the next review (FSRS) for every concept of the rated scene and never moves mastery. Its record carries `source: "self_rated"`, so a report can tell it apart from graded evidence. See [Learner model](learner-model.md#self-rating).

## Notices

A self-study lesson starts with a notice in the lesson's language (French for a French lesson, English otherwise). It joins a sentence on who wrote the keys with a sentence on what is assessed.

| Drafted by | First sentence | |---|---| | learner | "Self-authored lesson: quiz and spot-the-flaw keys were written by the learner (open book)." | | agent | "AI-drafted lesson from your sources, not checked by a teacher: each item cites its passage; tell the assistant about a key that looks wrong." | | agent, in a self-study lesson shipped with Studium | "Demo lesson shipped with Studium, drafted by an AI agent from Studium's documentation, not checked by a teacher: each item cites its passage; tell the assistant about a key that looks wrong." Its `authoring` block also carries `shipped: true`. |

| Judge | Second sentence | |---|---| | none | "Without a judge model, production scenes are not assessed: compare your answer with the provided reference and rate your recall; that rating schedules your reviews and never changes your mastery." | | configured | "Production scenes are assessed by the model." |

A lesson that holds a reproduction adds a third sentence: "Executed reproductions carry an external assessment."

« Discover Studium », the demo lesson shipped with Studium, has `mode: "teacher"`: it shows none of these notices, and what its first screen says about validation comes from its approval record. Its receipt records that the project's owner approved it without opening any scene.

The texts are defined in [`authoring.ts`](../../packages/lesson-session-host/src/authoring.ts).

## Sources and quotes

A lesson an assistant drafts with `create_lesson` cites a source passage for each graded item. Each quote must be a substring of the passage it names, 15 to 500 characters long. Only what a copy through a chat or a web page changes silently is folded: no-break spaces and runs of whitespace become one space, and typographic apostrophes become `'`. Accents, case and other punctuation stay significant. A quote that does not match is refused with a pointer to where it diverges, and the lesson is not written.

The licence given for each source is copied into the lesson's citations (`evidence.bibliographic_refs[].license`) and shown after the source's title; a source prepared without a licence gets no licence field.

The cited passages of a graded scene are released only after the answer, when the learner leaves the scene for good.

An exact quote proves a textual link, not that the item uses it correctly. That is why the agent-drafted notice asks the learner to tell the assistant about a key that looks wrong.

## Lint findings on authorship

`node tools/bundle_lint.mjs` adds these findings when `metadata.authoring` is present. WARN and INFO do not fail the run.

| Code | Level | When | |---|---|---| | `self_study_authoring` | INFO | always in self-study mode: mode, drafter, key classes | | `self_study_open_book` | WARN | author-keyed scenes whose key the learner wrote | | `self_study_agent_key` | WARN | author-keyed scenes whose key an agent drafted; check each against its passage | | `self_study_no_external_key` | WARN | no production and no externally grounded scene | | `learner_authored_validated` | INFO | a learner's lesson released as a teacher bundle |

## The approval record

A teacher records approval of a finished lesson with:

```bash .venv/bin/python tools/experience_packet.py approve --bundle path/to/lesson.json --validated-by "Teacher name" ```

The command refuses a lesson with remaining placeholders, with lint errors, or in self-study mode (which includes lessons drafted with `create_lesson`). It sets `validated_by` and `validated_at`, then writes `approval.json` (schema `studium-approval/1`) next to the lesson with the SHA-256 of the exact bytes of `lesson.json`, the reviewer, the date, an optional checklist (`--checklist KEY=VALUE ...`) and the lint summary.

The server reads the record and reports `approval.matches`: any edit to `lesson.json` after approval makes it false. A lesson distributed as a `.zip` carries its record as the member `approval.json`, bound to the bytes of the member `lesson.json`. The record is a file anyone with write access can edit; it documents a review, it is not a signature. Teachers can inspect a draft without seeing its keys with the MCP tool `review_lesson`. See [Review and approve](../teach/review-and-approve.md).

## Rule 003: a teacher before any release

The project's rule 003 is strict human-in-the-loop: no content is released to students without a teacher's validation. In practice:

- a teacher bundle reads as validated only with an approval record bound to its exact bytes (`approve` also writes the name in `validated_by`, which grants nothing on its own); - a self-study lesson, whether the learner or an agent drafted it, is for the learner who made it, and says so in its notice; an agent-drafted lesson in teacher mode, such as the demo shipped with Studium, has no notice and reads as validated only through its approval record, like any teacher bundle; - a learner's contribution reaches other learners only after a teacher's decision, see [Learner contributions](../teach/learner-contributions.md).

Studium makes provenance visible; it does not certify that a lesson is correct. The [privacy and limits](privacy-and-limits.md) page says what hashes, quotes and run checks do and do not prove.

# Learn a topic with your assistant

Tell your AI assistant what you want to learn and which sources to use. It builds a short lesson from those sources, plays it with you one question at a time, and brings the key ideas back over the following days. You need no teacher and no shell: the assistant talks to Studium through MCP (the Model Context Protocol, the way assistants call outside tools).
This works in Codex, Claude Code and any assistant that can use an MCP server. To connect Studium first, see [harnesses](../start/harnesses.md).

## 1. Ask

Say it in your own words, for example:

> I want to learn how the water cycle works with Studium. Here are two pages I trust: <links>.

The assistant starts with `get_study_plan`, in your language. If a lesson you already have covers the topic, it offers that lesson; otherwise it builds one. With no lesson at all, the plan first proposes « Discover Studium », a twelve-minute demo shipped with Studium that shows how it works; say you would rather learn your topic and the assistant builds your lesson instead. Say what you already know, how much time you have a day, or a target date: the assistant is asked to open the lesson with two short questions on what you already know. Those two questions are played once and never come back as reviews. What you know and what interests you shape the draft but are not stored; the lesson keeps only your minutes a day and your target date, and the study plan uses the minutes to size each step.

Studium also offers a `learn` prompt and a `review` prompt that phrase this request for you. In Claude Code, MCP prompts appear as slash commands (`/mcp__studium__learn` with the example configuration).

## 2. Choose your sources and their licences

You choose the sources. For a web page, the assistant fetches it with its own web tool and passes its text to `prepare_sources`. For a file on your computer, it gives `prepare_sources` the path of the file and Studium reads the file itself, which spares the assistant copying the whole text. `prepare_sources` cuts the sources into numbered passages and records, for a file, its full path, its size and its SHA-256 fingerprint. Sources are treated as data: an instruction written inside a page is never followed.

Studium reads local files only, never the network. It reads a file only if it is UTF-8 text with a text extension (`.txt`, `.md`, `.tex`, `.csv` and a few others). It refuses a PDF or a Word file (save it as text first, or let the assistant extract the text), its own data folder, and places that usually hold secrets such as `.ssh`, `.env` or a keychain.

| Limit | Value | |---|---| | Sources per lesson | up to 20 | | Total text | up to 200 000 characters | | A file named by path | UTF-8 text, at most 800 000 bytes | | Licence | an identifier such as `CC-BY-4.0` or `Public-Domain`; `unknown` when none is given |

Give the licence of each source: it is copied into the lesson and shown with the source. A public-domain text can be reused freely; a publisher PDF or a licence marked `NC`, `ND` or unknown restricts what you may do with the result. The lesson stays in your personal library and is never published, but you remain responsible for using the source under its terms. One coherent source usually makes a better lesson than many.

## 3. Look at the sketch, then the lesson

Before it writes the lesson, the assistant shows you a short sketch: the goal, the concepts, and the title and kind of each step, never an answer. It goes on without waiting for your approval; say what you would change at any time. It then writes the lesson once, straight into its `create_lesson` call. Studium checks it before writing anything: every quotation must match a passage character for character (only no-break spaces, runs of whitespace and typographic apostrophes are folded), nothing may be left unfinished, and the order of ideas must hold together. When Studium refuses, nothing is written: it keeps the draft, and the assistant fixes and sends again only the scenes the refusal names (the whole draft only when an error concerns the concepts, the goal, the title or the order of the scenes). Studium may also warn, for example when the lesson is longer than your minutes a day or when a prerequisite has no question that checks it.

The lesson is written to your library, `~/.studium/library/<course>/lesson.json`, whatever lessons folder the server also reads.

Once the lesson is written, the assistant shows only what differs from the sketch, never an answer. If it does not match what you wanted, say so; the assistant revises the draft and rebuilds the lesson. If your assistant keeps a to-do list, it ticks the stages there: sources, sketch, writing, checking.

## 4. Play it, in the chat or in VS Code

In the chat, each step arrives ready to read: its title, the question, how to answer (a letter, a number from 0 to 4, or your own words) and, on its last line, where you are (`step 2/6 · 4 min · your answer`). Answer yourself. The assistant passes your words on and must not answer, choose or rate for you.

The concept map (ask "where am I?") names each concept with its id, for example "Quantum numbers (`c-nombres-quantiques`): upcoming". If you already know a concept the map does not show as acquired, or doubt one it does, say so: the assistant contests it for you with `submit_response {kind: "contest", concept_id, claim}` (`known` or `unsure`), and never on its own. Your claim changes nothing about your mastery and skips no scene. The lesson opens with one line, "Check on “Quantum numbers”: 2 questions. Your claim changes nothing; the lesson then resumes where you were.", asks one or two check questions on that concept, graded like any answer (the last line says `check 1/2`), then resumes where you were. In forms, decline the form and say it in the conversation.

If each answer is slow to come, play the lesson in a new, short session on your assistant's fast model (in Claude Code, `claude --agent studium-lesson`): see [Keep answers fast](../start/fast-answers.md).

To play in VS Code instead, open the lesson from the **Lessons** view of the Studium extension: it appears there when it is ready, and VS Code tells you. You can also follow the link your assistant gives you (`vscode://holobiomicslab.studium-vscode/open?bundle=<absolute path>`). See [VS Code](../start/vscode.md). The pane keeps its own progress in VS Code's storage: answers given there do not appear in the study plan your assistant reads, and the reverse, except for Copilot with the Studium server the extension offers, which plays the pane's learner in that storage ([Connect Copilot](../start/copilot.md)).

## 5. Read the notice

The first screen of a lesson an assistant wrote carries a notice. Without a judge model, it reads:

> AI-drafted lesson from your sources, not checked by a teacher: each item cites its passage; tell the > assistant about a key that looks wrong. Without a judge model, production scenes are not assessed: compare your answer with the > provided reference and rate your recall; that rating schedules your reviews and never changes your mastery. Executed reproductions carry > an external assessment.

What it means in practice:

- **Who wrote the key.** The assistant wrote the correct answers. They cite the passages they rest on, so you can check them; a key can still be wrong. On a panel or a pane, the line over a quiz verdict says so too: "Assessed by the AI-drafted key — check it against the cited passage" (a lesson you wrote yourself says "Assessed by the key you wrote"; a teacher's lesson, "Assessed by the author's key"). - **What was assessed.** Quiz answers are checked against that key: ✓ when right, ✗ when wrong, and once you leave a question you answered wrong, the right answer is shown. Your written answers (explanations, comparisons, audits) are not scored unless a judge model is configured (`LITELLM_BASE_URL`). You get the key points and a model answer to compare with, never a keyword count that pretends to measure coverage. - **What your rating does.** After a written answer you rate your recall: `again`, `hard`, `good` or `easy`. That rating sets the date of the next review. It never raises or lowers your mastery.

No answer key, cited passage or model answer is shown before you answer, on any surface. They appear once you leave the question; a retry of the same question keeps them back. More in [honesty and provenance](../concepts/honesty-and-provenance.md).

## 6. Come back days later

Open a new conversation and ask "What should I study with Studium today?". The assistant calls `get_study_plan` in your language, which lists the reviews due, the lessons in progress and the next lesson, and names the one step to take now. `start_review_session` then plays every review due, across all your lessons. See [review over time](review-over-time.md). If Studium refused a draft of your lesson and no lesson was written for you since, the plan offers to finish it, after a lesson you have in progress, for 14 days, and only to you (the server plays only you); say you no longer want it and it is not offered again.

If you simply take a lesson up again, its first screen says so, and when reviews are due it proposes them at the start of the session, or at the first pause after it when the session started on a question, once per session:

> **Suggestion:** 1 concept to review today (suggestion `review_due:start`) > _You can accept, or say “later”._

Answer in your own words. If you accept, the assistant starts the review session; if you say "later", the lesson goes on. The same kind of proposal comes at a pause, never over a question: playing in forms when your client can show them, the concept map at the end of the lesson. Each one is made once.

Your progress survives restarts by default, under `~/.studium`. To find it again from another assistant, use the same data folder and set the same `STUDIUM_LEARNER_ID` in each assistant's server settings. The assistant does not name you: the server plays one learner.

## 7. Close or forget

| You say | The assistant calls | Effect | |---|---|---| | "Stop here for today." | `end_session` | Closes the session and keeps your progress. Starting the lesson again resumes it. | | "Erase my data for this lesson." | `forget_session {session_id}` | Erases your progress in this lesson, its experiment journal, and your cross-lesson profile and study record. Cannot be undone. | | "Erase all my Studium data." | `forget_session {learner_id}` | The same, plus your progress in every other lesson and the drafts Studium kept for you, without a lesson open. Cannot be undone. |

The assistant then shows what was erased and what stays. Forgetting does not delete the lessons in your library (`~/.studium/library/<course>/`) or the prepared sources (`~/.studium/library/_sources/`), nor the conversation your assistant keeps. Remove those yourself if you want them gone. See [privacy and limits](../concepts/privacy-and-limits.md).

## Sample conversation

> **You:** I want to learn the water cycle with Studium, from this encyclopedia page. It is CC-BY-SA. > > **Assistant:** I prepared 4 passages from the page and drafted a lesson. Outline: 1. The water cycle > (introduction) · 2. Evaporation (quiz) · 3. Condensation and clouds (explain back) · 4. From rain to rivers > (comparison). Shall I start it? > > **You:** Yes. > > **Assistant:** *AI-drafted lesson from your sources, not checked by a teacher …* Step 2 of 4. What makes ocean > water evaporate? A, B or C? > > **You:** B. > > **Assistant:** Right. Step 3 of 4: explain in your own words how a cloud forms. > > **You:** The vapour rises, cools and turns into droplets. > > **Assistant:** Answer recorded; no judge assessed it. Compare it with these key points and the model answer. > How well did you recall it: again, hard, good or easy? > > **You:** Good. > > **Assistant:** Rating recorded. Next review: <date>. It schedules your reviews and never changes your mastery.

## Going further

- Step by step with a real source: [learn a topic in a conversation](../tutorials/learn-a-topic-in-a-conversation.md). - The same route with the Python packet tools, for full control: [self-study from references](../tutorials/self-study-from-references.md). - Every tool and its arguments: [MCP tools](../reference/mcp-tools.md); the code is in [apps/lesson-mcp/src/authoring-tools.ts](../../apps/lesson-mcp/src/authoring-tools.ts) and [apps/lesson-mcp/src/server.ts](../../apps/lesson-mcp/src/server.ts).

# Review over time

Come back to Studium on any later day and one question, "what should I study now?", gets one answer: the reviews due, the lessons in progress and the next step. A review session then brings back every concept due, across all your lessons, just before you are likely to forget it. This is spaced review: each successful recall pushes the next one further away. Studium schedules it with FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler), a model of how memory fades; see the [glossary](../concepts/glossary.md).

## Ask for your study plan

In a chat, say "What should I study with Studium today?" or use the `review` prompt. The assistant calls `get_study_plan` in your language (French or English; without one, the language of your last lesson) and shows the plan as it comes:

| Section | What it lists | |---|---| | **To review** | Concepts you mastered whose recall is now due, most urgent first | | **To relearn** | Concepts graded below the mastery threshold and due again | | **Due for review** | Concepts due that only your self-rating scheduled: nothing measured them, so they are not called weak | | **In progress** | Lessons started and not finished, with the number of steps done | | **Next lesson** | The next lesson of a course you follow, or the newest lesson you have not opened | | **Now** | The one step to take |

The step to take follows a fixed order: play the reviews due, otherwise continue a lesson in progress, otherwise start the next lesson, otherwise, when you have no lesson of your own, the demo lesson shipped with Studium (« Discover Studium », once), otherwise build a lesson from your sources (when you have none), otherwise wait, with the date of the next review. A concept that no lesson can replay as a question stays listed, marked "no review question covers it yet", but is never proposed as the next step. Dates are calendar days in the time zone of the machine that runs Studium.

If you gave your minutes a day when your assistant built a lesson, the plan sizes the step with them: a lesson longer than that is proposed in several sittings, and a review session is cut to what fits today.

In VS Code, the status bar shows how many concepts are waiting ("Studium · 2 to review" when all are due reviews, "Studium · 3 to work on" otherwise); its tooltip and the sidebar keep the three groups apart: to review, to take up again, not measured yet. The pane counts its own progress only; see [learn with your assistant](learn-with-your-assistant.md#4-play-it-in-the-chat-or-in-vs-code).

## Play a review session

`start_review_session` builds one short session with a question for each concept due, taken from the lesson you learned it in, among the scenes whose main concept it is. It prefers a question other than the one you answered last time and, when no judge model is configured, a question graded against a key. It plays like a lesson: you answer in your own words or by choosing, and rate your recall when asked. At most 50 questions per session.

- Questions come from quiz, spot-the-flaw, explain-back, comparison, summary-audit and prompt-practice scenes. Reading scenes are not replayed, nor the opening diagnostic of a lesson ("what do you already know?"), nor scenes that depend on a run you made inside the lesson. - Answers update your review memory and your mastery. A review session is never recorded as a lesson completed. - When nothing is due, you get the date of the next review instead. A concept due whose lesson is no longer on disk is named as one that cannot be reviewed any more.

At the end you see the next review date and three lists: **Consolidated** (at least three graded answers and a mastery at the review threshold), **Practised** (graded, with the number of answers, not yet consolidated) and **Not measured yet** (nothing graded them).

## What schedules a review, and what does not

| What happened | Schedules a review | Changes mastery | |---|---|---| | A quiz or spot-the-flaw answer | Yes: wrong reads as "again", right after a hint as "hard", right as "good" | Yes | | A written answer no judge assessed, then your self-rating | Yes, from your rating | No | | A written answer no judge assessed, not rated | No | No | | A written answer assessed by a judge model | No self-rating is asked; the judge's assessment is the graded evidence | Yes | | A reading scene or a confidence check | No | No |

Your self-rating (`again`, `hard`, `good`, `easy`) is your own judgement after comparing your answer with the key points and the model answer. It tells the scheduler how soon to ask again, for every concept of the question you rated. It is never treated as proof that you know the concept, which is why such concepts appear under **Due for review** and not **To relearn**. An answer nobody graded is not counted as a recall, neither a success nor a failure. Background: [the learner model](../concepts/learner-model.md).

## Where your data lives

Progress is durable by default: it survives a restart of the assistant or the computer.

| What | Where | |---|---| | Lessons your assistant writes | `~/.studium/library/<course>/lesson.json`, whatever `BUNDLES_ROOT` names | | Prepared sources | `~/.studium/library/_sources/` | | Drafts of unfinished lessons | `~/.studium/library/_drafts/`, until the lesson is written, discarded, or 14 days old | | Progress, mastery, review memory, study record | `~/.studium/data/`, one folder per learner pseudonym | | Pseudonym secret | `~/.studium/data/.studium-secret`, created with a new data folder | | VS Code pane progress | VS Code's own extension storage |

`STUDIUM_HOME` moves `~/.studium`; `STUDIUM_DATA_DIR` moves the data folder alone; `STUDIUM_EPHEMERAL=1` keeps everything in memory, and the assistant then warns you that progress is lost at restart. See [configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

Folders on disk are named by a pseudonym computed from your learner id and the secret, never by your id itself. To move your data to another machine, copy the whole data folder, secret included: without it your folders can no longer be matched to your id. Set the same `STUDIUM_LEARNER_ID` in every assistant to keep one history.

## Limits

- Reviews only exist for what was graded or self-rated: a lesson read without answering schedules nothing. - Review dates are an estimate from a model of forgetting, not a guarantee. - Erasing a lesson's data with `forget_session` also erases your cross-lesson memory and study record; the lessons in your library and their sources stay until you delete them. Details: [privacy and limits](../concepts/privacy-and-limits.md).

The study plan code is in [packages/lesson-session-host/src/study-plan.ts](../../packages/lesson-session-host/src/study-plan.ts) and the review session in [packages/lesson-session-host/src/review-session.ts](../../packages/lesson-session-host/src/review-session.ts).

# Privacy and limits

Studium keeps learner state on the learner's machine and collects as little as it can. That does not mean everything stays local: an assistant connected to a remote model sends what it reads to its provider. This page tells you where each piece of data lives, how to erase it, and what Studium's evidence does and does not prove. Read it before a class pilot.

## Where your data lives

The MCP server (`apps/lesson-mcp`) uses these defaults. Each can be changed with an environment variable; see the [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.md).

| What | Default location | Change it with | |---|---|---| | Root of your library and data | `~/.studium` | `STUDIUM_HOME` | | Lessons written for you | `<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/<course>/lesson.json`, whatever `BUNDLES_ROOT` names | `STUDIUM_HOME`; `BUNDLES_ROOT` only adds a folder searched first | | Sources prepared for those lessons (their passages, and for a file read by path its full path, size and SHA-256) | `<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_sources/` | `STUDIUM_HOME` | | A draft Studium refused, kept so the assistant resends only the faulty scenes (see *A kept draft* below) | `<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_drafts/` | `STUDIUM_HOME` | | Your progress | `<STUDIUM_HOME>/data` | `STUDIUM_DATA_DIR` | | Nothing on disk, memory only | off | `STUDIUM_EPHEMERAL=1` | | The one learner the server plays (an id an assistant passes is ignored) | `anonymous` | `STUDIUM_LEARNER_ID` | | Play the `learner_id` of each call (shared computer, evaluations) | off | `STUDIUM_LEARNERS=several` |

Inside the data folder, each learner has a folder named by a pseudonym, never by their id:

| File | Content | |---|---| | `<pseudonym>/profile.json` | cross-lesson profile, including review memory | | `<pseudonym>/study.json` | where the learner studied, and where they last answered a step (`answered_on`: the browser, the VS Code pane, a panel, the Claude Code pane or the chat), so that the next lesson is offered there first | | `<pseudonym>/status.json` | where the session being played stands (lesson title, step, minutes left), for an assistant's status line; removed when the session closes | | `<pseudonym>/<lesson>/state-<lesson>.json` | lesson state and mastery | | `<pseudonym>/<lesson>/events.jsonl` | the session's event log | | `<pseudonym>/<lesson>/mastery/*.jsonld` | mastery claims, when a concept is certified | | `<pseudonym>/<lesson>/telemetry.jsonl` | only with telemetry consent; written as the learner acts, opened by a record of the consent declared through `STUDIUM_TELEMETRY_CONSENT` |

With `STUDIUM_EPHEMERAL=1` and no `STUDIUM_DATA_DIR`, progress is lost when the server stops, and `get_server_info` and `start_lesson_session` say so.

When you tell your assistant what you already know, what interests you, how many minutes a day you have or a target date, the first two only shape the lesson's draft and are not stored. The lesson file keeps the minutes a day and the target date (`metadata.authoring.learner_profile`), and your study record keeps the minutes; a lesson file you share carries them with it.

### A kept draft

When Studium refuses a lesson draft for what it says, it keeps the draft in `<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_drafts/` so that the assistant sends back only the faulty scenes. The kept draft holds the lesson as the assistant wrote it, answer keys included, the errors found in it, the sources it rests on (by their SHA-256) and the pseudonym of the learner it was written for. Of your learner profile it keeps only the minutes a day and the target date: what you already know and what interests you stay out, even under a misspelled field name, and so do the errors about them.

The study plan offers to finish it only to the learner it was refused for, after a lesson they have in progress. The server plays one learner, so the draft is kept for them even when that learner is `anonymous`. With `STUDIUM_LEARNERS=several`, when a call gives no `learner_id` and `STUDIUM_LEARNER_ID` is not set, no learner is known: the draft serves only the resend in the same conversation and is offered to no one, so a computer several learners share never shows one learner's goal or file to another.

It is erased when a lesson is written for that learner (or from the same sources with no learner named), when the learner says they no longer want it, when they erase their data with `forget_session {learner_id}`, which also erases the drafts kept for no learner, and in any case after 14 days.

The VS Code extension runs its own server with its data in the extension's VS Code storage, separate from `<STUDIUM_HOME>/data`.

### Pseudonyms

A pseudonym is an HMAC of the learner id. The secret is `STUDIUM_PSEUDO_SECRET` when set; otherwise a fresh data folder gets its own secret file, `<data dir>/.studium-secret` (permissions 0600). Back it up with the data folder: without it, the learner folders can no longer be matched to their learners. A data folder created before this file existed keeps the former shared secret so nobody loses progress; anyone holding such a folder and a learner's id can recompute the pseudonym, so set `STUDIUM_PSEUDO_SECRET` for it.

## Who controls what

| Space | What it can hold | Who controls retention | |---|---|---| | Studium server | Session state and, by default, the durable profile | Studium settings and forget commands | | Local HTTP API | Active sessions and retry receipts, in the server's memory | The local user; the token opens every session of that server | | Assistant and its provider | Prompts, content sent, tool calls, history | The client's and provider's settings and terms | | Experiment folder | Code, data, logs, receipts, chosen observations | The folder's user | | Shared course | Authorised sources, plan, assets, answer criteria | The teacher and distribution rules | | Class telemetry | Consented events | The pilot lead and the collection policy |

## Defaults to keep

- Telemetry consent is off: `studium.telemetryConsent` is `false` in VS Code, and the server writes telemetry only when `STUDIUM_TELEMETRY_CONSENT` is set and state is durable. Do not turn collection on to fix a connection problem. - Use a demonstration id, not a real name, for onboarding. - Keep `studium.assets` on `vendor` so rendering libraries load locally; the `cdn` option contacts an external server. - Keep `studium.showMastery` off and the graph in the student view during an exercise: review views can reveal more than the exercise intends.

## Answer keys

Scenes are served without their keys, and `lesson-server` redacts keys over HTTP. But an agent with access to the repository or to the raw `lesson.json` can read them: redaction on the wire does not protect local files. The Studium skills tell the assistant never to read keys in the raw bundle.

## Forget and export

| Action | What it erases | What it keeps | |---|---|---| | `end_session` | nothing | lesson state and cross-lesson memory | | `forget_session {session_id}` | this learner's durable state for the lesson (answers, lesson state, experiment journal), their cross-lesson profile, study record and status file; irreversible | their progress in other lessons, which it names | | `forget_session {learner_id}` | the same for every lesson the learner opened, with no session needed, and the drafts kept for them or for no learner; their live sessions close; irreversible | nothing of the learner's progress; another learner's drafts | | VS Code "Studium: Forget my data" | the extension's storage, its run-trust memory and last lesson, after closing every lesson server the extension started and a confirmation | an assistant's data in `<STUDIUM_HOME>/data`, which it names and does not touch |

`forget_session` answers with what it erased and what stays on disk: the lessons of the learner's library (`<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/<course>/`) and the sources prepared for them (`<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_sources/`), and for one lesson the drafts of unfinished lessons (`<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_drafts/`). The assistant shows that list; delete those folders by hand to remove them too. The install's pseudonym secret also stays: it holds no learner data.

No forget command reaches the assistant's history, experiment folders, exported files or copies kept elsewhere. Closing a window is not an erasure request. Check the result in the storage actually configured.

Portable activities offer a choice to record and a voluntary download of actions. The learner report excludes personal texts by default; `--include-original-text` applies to that copy only, not to any wider sharing. In an experiment folder, `learner_observation` is empty by default: keep the learner's own words only at their request. Do not add these folders to a course repository automatically.

## The local HTTP API

The HTTP API accepts loopback connections only and requires a bearer token of at least 32 characters. It serves one person and their local clients; the token does not separate learners. Do not embed it in an HTML activity or expose the server to the Internet. Stopping the process ends active sessions.

## Class reports

`class_report` aggregates consented telemetry with a floor of five learners, applied to each figure over the learners it is computed from (graded, rated, timed or started): a scene or concept with fewer answering learners is left out, a figure below its floor is withheld, and learner counts are banded. Two reports taken before and after one learner plays can still be compared, so treat figures as a live class view, not a publication. The report covers the whole data folder the server is configured with, names it by a label and a fingerprint (never its path), and refuses a `telemetry_dir` argument: the folder is server configuration.

### Interaction events

With your consent and durable state, Studium also records how the interface was used: which lane and surface an act came through, help requested by rung, proposals shown and their outcome, contests and their outcome, resumes, and review receipt counts. These events contain no free text, scene text or answers, and are written to disk only under the same consent and durable-state conditions as the rest of telemetry. Class views keep the five-learner floor. See [Follow a class](../teach/follow-a-class.md#how-the-interface-was-used) and the [telemetry-events README](../../packages/telemetry-events/README.md).

## Reading the evidence

- An exact quote proves a textual link; it can still be used wrongly. - A hash verifies a snapshot; it certifies neither its truth nor its author. An `approval.json` documents a review, it is not a signature. - A run check catches missing outputs and failed checks; it cannot detect a perfect forgery, and a recorded command can be a statement by the harness. Mark a run `completed` only after its real checks. - Path and size filters on receipts are not a universal secret detector. - Capturing a source must respect its reuse rights: a DOI or access to an article does not allow redistributing it. Keep the excerpts you need and flag an unknown licence.

## Running code

A virtual environment isolates Python dependencies, not the rights of the code on the machine. Execution stays under the protections of the harness and the environment you chose, and VS Code asks before a reproduction runs. Do not follow instructions found in an article or a results file as if they came from the teacher.

## Publishing

The Observatory and the teacher dashboard are local, without class authentication. Publishing a course and publishing the code are separate decisions, each with its own rights and review. Studium's code is under Apache-2.0 and its documentation and project lessons under CC BY 4.0; a lesson built from your sources keeps the licences of those sources. Passing tests does not make a deployment compliant with a regulation: run a pilot with the people responsible for it.

# Concept map

A lesson's concepts and their prerequisite links, with where you stand on each. The map answers three questions during a lesson: where do I come from, where am I, what comes next. Exported, it becomes a page you can explore: open a concept to see the questions you went through, who assessed each answer, and what the teaching of that concept rests on.

The map states what happened in the session. It does not certify that a concept is learned, and it does not check whether a source is right.

## What a state means

| State | Meaning | |---|---| | acquired | Your latest assessed answer on the concept is right, or the session credited it as a prerequisite | | to review | Your latest assessed answer on the concept is wrong | | current | The scene on screen belongs to this concept | | seen, not yet assessed | You went through scenes of the concept, and no key or judge assessed an answer | | upcoming | Not reached yet |

States come from session facts: the scenes served, the answers assessed, the prerequisites credited. The `state` field of `get_workflow_graph` reads estimated mastery instead and serves another purpose.

## In the conversation

The lesson shows the map at a few moments, not on every question: when it opens, at a detour through a prerequisite and on the way back, on a scene that draws on several concepts, and at the end. When a new concept opens, one line says where you are. Ask for the map at any time: your assistant calls `get_workflow_graph` and shows `concept_map`. A harness that draws diagrams can render `concept_map.mermaid`.

## In the lesson panel

In the lesson panel and in the Claude Code pane, « Concept map » opens the map as a list under the scene. Nothing is submitted and the scene stays where it is. Each concept says its state in words and what it needs first. « Evidence and scope » shows what the state establishes, what it does not, and the answers behind it: the day, who assessed the answer, the result and the hints taken. Where a concept can be checked, a button states your claim (« I know it » or « I am not sure »): the lesson then asks one or two check questions and says what they showed. A question whose answer you have already been shown is not asked again: when only such questions are left on a concept, it cannot be checked again in this lesson. A concept the session has not shown yet cannot be contested until it is reached. Your claim alone changes nothing. « Close the map » puts the list away. The panel does not draw the graph; the exported page below does.

## Export an interactive page

Ask your assistant to export the map. It calls `export_concept_map`, which writes a record under your library (`<STUDIUM_HOME>/library/_exports/concept-maps/`) and returns its path and SHA-256. Then, from the repository root:

```bash .venv/bin/python tools/concept_map_report.py export RECORD.json reports/concept-map --expect-sha256 SHA256 ```

```bash .venv/bin/python tools/concept_map_report.py verify reports/concept-map ```

Open `reports/concept-map/index.html`. The page needs no network and no server. Your assistant's procedure for all of this is the `studium-concept-map` skill ([Skills](../start/skills.md)).

| On the page | What it does | |---|---| | A concept of the graph | Opens its panel: prerequisites, your steps, sources, trace nodes | | A step of the session path | Opens the concept of that step and highlights the step | | Viewpoint: Learner | Colours concepts by state; shows your steps and the path travelled | | Viewpoint: Teacher | Shows the structure, what each concept rests on and, when attached, the class figures | | Concepts shown | Dims the concepts of a state |

The record holds no learner identifier and none of your words: results, not answers. For each answer it also keeps the day, the hints you took before it and whether you then rated your own recall, and, for each concept you contested (« I know it », « I am not sure »), what the check questions showed. It stays on your machine until you share the folder. `forget_session` does not delete exports; it names the folder so you can delete it yourself.

The concept map exported after a session (synthetic learner): where each concept stands, and the answers behind it. ## What a concept rests on For each scene of a concept, the panel gives the kind of key (written by the author, a production compared with a reference, grounded by a run, or not graded), the sources cited and where each comes from: a web page, a publication, a supplied document, or a conversation with an AI assistant. A passage is quoted only once you have left the scene that cites it, because a passage can state the key of its question. The header says who drafted the lesson and whether a teacher validated this exact version (a lesson changed since its approval says so).

For a lesson drafted from a conversation, read [learn with your assistant](learn-with-your-assistant.md): what an assistant asserted there was not checked.

## The teacher viewpoint and class figures

A teacher who wants the figures of a class on the map exports the class report with the teacher tool `class_report`, saves its JSON, and passes it (the JSON written by `tools/class_report.py` also works, run with `--bundle path/to/lesson.json` so its rows are named by concept):

```bash .venv/bin/python tools/concept_map_report.py export RECORD.json reports/class-map --class-report class-report.json ```

Each concept then shows its success rate (over the graded answers, whose number is given when it is lower than the answers' own), hint reliance, calibration gap and mean time, and the concepts to reteach first are marked. Figures under the learner floor of `class_report` are not shown, and no individual figure exists in that report. The page still holds the session path of the record it was built from: for a page without any learner's path, export the record from a session just started.

## Provenance files

| File | Standard | Content | |---|---|---| | `sources/concept-map-record.json` | Studium record | The record the server wrote, copied unchanged | | `astra.yaml` | ASTRA 0.0.14 | The record as a declared artifact, the choices made (state rule, passages quoted, class figures) and technical findings | | `trace/exploration_tree.yaml` | ARA 0.1.0 | The session path: one node per step, one pivot per detour | | `course_provenance.myst.md` | MySTRA | The same provenance as a readable page, with the map | | `report.json`, `checks.json` | Studium | The summary and its limits; the digest of every file and the ASTRA validator's result |

Your results stay in the declared record; they are never written as custom ASTRA fields. To read the package in the Observatory, point its course root at the parent folder, as for a [learner report](learner-report.md#open-and-verify).

Verification recomputes the summary, the ASTRA document, the trace and both pages from the record, runs the installed `astra-tools` validator and checks every digest. The manifest is unsigned: it detects stale or changed files, and someone who can rewrite the whole folder can rewrite its digests too.

## Limits

- Whether a map helps learning has not been measured. - A lesson resumed after a server restart keeps its latest steps and their results (the saved history is bounded); who assessed each earlier answer and how the session routed are recorded only for the steps played since the restart. - Mermaid rendering in each harness was not checked by eye; the list form is always present.

# Student guide

Studium plays a lesson one step at a time and chooses what comes next from your answers: a hint, a detour through a prerequisite, or the next idea. An AI assistant can explain a tool, prepare a calculation or draw a graph for you. **Your prediction, your reasoning and your conclusion stay yours.** This page covers what to do in a lesson, how to use the assistant without handing it the work, and how to stop and resume.

## Before your first session

Ask your teacher for the course lesson (a `lesson.json` with its assets), the Studium version and which experiments you may run. A PDF alone is not a playable lesson. To try right away, use the `atomistique-l1` lesson shipped in `fixtures/`.

1. Follow the [quickstart](../start/quickstart.md). 2. Choose where to play: the [VS Code lesson pane](../start/vscode.md), which needs no AI account, or an assistant such as Codex, Claude Code, Copilot or OpenCode over MCP ([harnesses](../start/harnesses.md)). 3. Play the [first lesson tutorial](../tutorials/first-lesson.md).

If your teacher gives you a portable activity (`index.html`), open it in a browser: nothing to install.

Class telemetry is off unless you opt in. While you try things out, use a test learner id rather than your real name; your teacher explains the rules of a class pilot before any collection. To learn without a teacher, from your own sources, see [learn with your assistant](learn-with-your-assistant.md).

## What to do in each scene

| Scene | Your part | |---|---| | Introduction, concept | Read, look at the figures, then continue | | Quiz | Reason first, then choose; ask for a hint if you need one | | Confidence check | Give your own confidence, from 0 to 4 | | Reproduction | Read the protocol, predict, then examine results that were really run | | Spot the flaw, summary audit, AI critique | Tie each objection to a fact or a piece of evidence | | Explain back, comparison | Write your own formulation and its limits | | Discussion | Build the argument over several turns | | Prompt practice, communication | Draft, then improve your own proposal |

Not every course uses every type; see [scene types](../concepts/scene-types.md). The pane shows the right controls for each scene. In a chat, each step tells you how to answer: a letter, a number, or your own words.

## If you are stuck

Try your own answer first, then use the help ladder in order: reread the step, ask for a hint, ask for an explanation, and read the reference. An explanation becomes available after you have tried an answer and hands your question to the assistant; the reference comes with the verdict, after your answer. Rereading costs nothing, while a hint reduces the mastery credit of a correct answer and brings its review sooner. See [language and supports](language-and-supports.md) for the other kinds of help you can request.

## Look back at a step already done

In the VS Code pane and the browser player, each step of the lesson's main path you already did is a numbered button under the progress rail. It shows that step again as it was, with your answer and the feedback you got, read only: going back never rewinds the lesson, and nothing you do there changes your progress, your mastery or your reviews. **Back to where I was** returns to your current step, as you left it. See [What you see](../start/vscode.md#what-you-see) for the details.

## See your concept map

The concept map shows each concept's state, what it needs first, the path you travelled and the assessed answers behind it. Open it in the lesson panel or pane, in forms, or ask in the conversation for the map returned by `get_workflow_graph`. On a concept you have reached, you can say that you know it or are unsure: Studium asks one or two check questions and reports their outcome; the claim alone never raises mastery or skips a scene. See [Concept map](concept-map.md).

## Use the assistant without giving it the activity

Requests that keep you in charge:

> Give me a hint about the approach, then wait for my attempt.

> Show these data with their units. Ask me first what I predict when the threshold changes. Keep the reference > visible next to the variant.

> Here is my explanation: […]. Ask me one question that tests its limit, without replacing my text before I > submit it.

> Explain the last adaptation with the Studium tool. Separate what it reports from your own interpretation.

A hint lowers the mastery credit of your eventual answer; it is still worth asking when you are stuck. A detour sends you to a prerequisite and then back. Mastery figures are a learning aid, not an official grade or a diagnosis. See [the learner model](../concepts/learner-model.md).

## Experiment with an article or a capsule

Follow the [agentic experiment tutorial](../tutorials/agentic-experiment.md): pick a question, predict an effect, run a reference, change one factor and judge the difference. Record your prediction before seeing any result in the [experiment journal](experiment-journal.md).

The assistant may search documentation or read a skill, but it must say what it actually consulted and ran. Check units, data, edge cases and provenance: a graph an AI produced can be wrong. Keep outputs in your experiment folder. A capsule marked `type-checked` is not a successful run. If a dependency is missing or a calculation fails, keep that failure; never ask the assistant to make up a result. In VS Code, a reproduction asks you to confirm the exact command before anything runs.

## Language, representations and reports

Ask for another language at any time ("Continue in French"); your answers and the original sources are kept as they are. You can ask for a readable equation, a diagram, a chemical structure or a plain-text explanation. See [language and supports](language-and-supports.md).

To keep a record of your own actions, see the [learner report](learner-report.md) and the [activity-to-report tutorial](../tutorials/activity-to-report.md). You choose what goes in; producing a report does not send it to your teacher.

## Stop and resume

- **Pause.** Say "stop here"; the assistant calls `end_session`, which closes the session and keeps your progress. Closing a window alone does not erase anything. - **Resume.** Start the same lesson with the same learner id: Studium resumes at the first unfinished step. A finished lesson starts again from the beginning as a retake. - **Several places.** The VS Code pane and an assistant keep separate progress, except Copilot with the server the Studium extension offers, which shares the pane's: same folder, same learner. Two assistants share it when they use the same data folder and learner id. - **Erase.** Ask the assistant to forget your data for a lesson, or all your data (`forget_session`); it then tells you what stays on disk. See [learn with your assistant](learn-with-your-assistant.md#7-close-or-forget). In VS Code, **Studium: Forget my data** erases what the extension keeps, not an assistant's data. Experiment folders and the assistant's own history follow their own retention rules.

Spaced reviews bring concepts back over the following days: see [review over time](review-over-time.md). If something goes wrong, see [troubleshooting](../start/troubleshooting.md) and send your teacher only a small, anonymised example. Privacy details: [privacy and limits](../concepts/privacy-and-limits.md).

# Connect your assistant

Studium runs as an MCP server that your AI assistant starts on your computer. Once it is connected, you can say "I want to learn X with Studium" and the assistant builds, plays and schedules your lessons through Studium's tools. This page helps you pick the page for your client, then shows how to check the connection.

## Before you start

The assistant's client is called a *harness* (see the [glossary](../concepts/glossary.md)). The server talks over stdio: it opens no port and shows no web page. A configuration starts it in one of two ways:

| Way | Command | When | |---|---|---| | From npm | `npx -y studium-mcp` | the usual way; needs only Node 20 or later (see [Installation](installation.md#add-the-server-to-your-assistant)) | | From a file | `node /path/to/studium/apps/studium-vscode/dist/lesson-mcp.cjs` | from a checkout after `pnpm --filter studium-vscode build`, or with a `lesson-mcp.cjs` downloaded from a release (use its own path) |

Each client page gives the `npx` form first and the checkout form second. Replace `/path/to/studium` with the absolute path of your checkout. If `npx` cannot reach npm, see [Where the packages are](installation.md#where-the-packages-are).

You meet two environment variables first:

| Setting | Effect | |---|---| | `BUNDLES_ROOT` | Leave it unset (recommended): lessons live in `~/.studium/library`, progress in `~/.studium/data`. Set `BUNDLES_ROOT=/path/to/studium/fixtures` to play the demo lessons shipped with the repository; lessons your assistant builds still go to `~/.studium/library`. | | `LITELLM_BASE_URL=""` | No judge model, even if your shell defines one (see [Judge model](../reference/configuration.md#judge-model-optional)). |

`STUDIUM_EPHEMERAL=1` keeps progress in memory only, for a demo or a test. All variables are listed in [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

The files in [docs/examples](../examples/) are complete examples, in the checkout form, that add `BUNDLES_ROOT` for the demo lessons: [codex.toml](../examples/codex.toml), [mcp.claude.json](../examples/mcp.claude.json), [mcp.vscode.json](../examples/mcp.vscode.json) and [opencode-v2.json](../examples/opencode-v2.json). Merge them into your client's file; never overwrite other servers already configured there.

## Choose your client

With the Studium extension for VS Code, **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** connects Mistral Vibe, Codex, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and OpenCode in one click, with no Node and no terminal: it writes one `studium` entry into each assistant's own file, running the server the extension carries. Copilot in VS Code has the server already. Each page below starts with that route, then gives the manual one.

| Client | Where its configuration lives | Page | |---|---|---| | Codex | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** in VS Code (no Node), or `~/.codex/config.toml`, or `codex mcp add` | [Connect Codex](codex.md) | | Claude Code | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** in VS Code (no Node), the `studium` plugin, `claude mcp add`, or `.mcp.json` at the project root | [Connect Claude Code](claude-code.md) | | Copilot in VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` | [Connect Copilot in VS Code](copilot.md) | | OpenCode | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** in VS Code (no Node), or `opencode.jsonc` at the project root | [Connect OpenCode](opencode.md) | | Cursor | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** in VS Code (no Node), or `.cursor/mcp.json` or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | [Connect Cursor](cursor.md) | | Mistral Vibe | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** or **Studium: Connect Mistral Vibe** in VS Code (no Node), or `~/.vibe/config.toml`, or `vibe mcp add` | [Connect Mistral Vibe](vibe.md) | | Claude Desktop | **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** in VS Code (no Node), or `claude_desktop_config.json` | [below](#claude-desktop) | | A script or a custom client | no MCP configuration | [HTTP API](../reference/http-api.md) and

## Claude Desktop

Claude Desktop reads `claude_desktop_config.json`, in `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/` on macOS and in `%APPDATA%\Claude\` on Windows. With the Studium extension for VS Code, **Studium: Connect an Assistant…** with **Claude Desktop** ticked writes the entry for you, with no Node; then quit and reopen Claude Desktop. Checked on 26 November 2026 on macOS: the entry it writes started the server with its 40 tools; Claude Desktop itself was not tried yet. By hand, merge this into the file, then restart the app:

```json { "mcpServers": { "studium": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "studium-mcp"], "env": { "LITELLM_BASE_URL": "" } } } } ```

From a checkout, use `"command": "node"` and `"args": ["/path/to/studium/apps/studium-vscode/dist/lesson-mcp.cjs"]`.

## Check the connection

A configuration entry, or a skill the client discovered, does not prove the server is connected. Ask:

```text Call the Studium tool get_server_info and tell me the version, the build date, the number of tools and whether my progress is durable. Then call get_study_plan. ```

The answer should list 40 tools (25 lesson, 5 study, 3 authoring, 2 teacher tools, 1 form tool, 3 panel tools and 1 companion tool; see [MCP tools](../reference/mcp-tools.md)) and `persistence.durable: true`. If `durable` is false, progress is lost when the server stops. When the server connects, the assistant also receives Studium's instructions (relay each `display_markdown` as it is, wait for your own answer, never answer or rate for you) and two prompts, `learn` and `review`, in clients that support MCP prompts.

# Teacher guide

Studium helps you turn sources you trust into a lesson your students can play, with every graded item tied to a passage you can check. You decide what is taught, what the sources allow you to claim, and when a lesson reaches students. A lesson that passes every technical check stays a draft until you approve it; that human decision before any distribution is the project's rule 003.

This page walks through the whole journey and links to the page for each step. To have your assistant guide you through it, load the `studium-teacher` skill (see [skills](../start/skills.md)).

## The journey at a glance

| Step | What you do | Result | Page | |---|---|---|---| | Prepare | Choose a question, an audience and the sources you may use | A pilot plan | [below](#prepare-the-activity) | | Author | Have your assistant draft the lesson from captured passages | A checked draft | [Author a lesson](author-a-lesson.md) | | Review | Read the plan, the quotes, the keys and the provenance | Your corrections | [Review and approve](review-and-approve.md) | | Approve | Record your decision for the exact lesson file | `approval.json` | [Review and approve](review-and-approve.md#approve-the-exact-file) | | Distribute | Give students the lesson folder | Lessons in their library | [below](#distribute-a-lesson) | | Follow a class | Read class-level aggregates, never a single student | A class report | [Follow a class](follow-a-class.md) | | Moderate | Review what learners propose to add | Community items | [Learner contributions](learner-contributions.md) |

Approval also writes a receipt of the items you opened and your verdict on each graded item. To send a lesson back without approving it, record a returned receipt instead; see [Review and approve](review-and-approve.md#approve-the-exact-file).

The teacher dashboard library: each lesson with who holds its answer keys and its review status. ## Before you start 1. Install Studium: [installation](../start/installation.md). 2. Play a lesson yourself to see what a student receives: [first lesson](../tutorials/first-lesson.md). 3. Connect your assistant (Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, OpenCode or another MCP client): [harnesses](../start/harnesses.md). No extra model provider is needed to author through it. 4. Follow the [literature to course tutorial](../tutorials/literature-to-course.md) once, on the shipped example, before using your own material.

## Prepare the activity

Start from a question that asks for more than a computed output, for example "Is a high spectral similarity enough to identify a molecule?". Then separate:

- the concept to understand and the task to carry out; - the expected observation and the limit to discuss; - a new case to check transfer.

Decide the pilot: audience, prerequisites, duration, judgement question, what students may explore, which materials are allowed and how results are returned. A framing prompt for your assistant can look like this:

> Prepare a Studium draft for [audience], in [duration], on [question]. Use only the passages > and materials in the packet. Separate the paper's results, hypotheses and synthetic data. > Ask for a prediction before any run, a comparison and a transfer question. Flag missing > evidence. Mark nothing as approved and invent no capsule result.

The [use cases](../tutorials/use-cases.md) show complete examples (spectral annotation, diagnosing an analysis, robustness, photographs in archaeology). Ready-made interactive starters are in [activity templates](activity-templates.md); figures, equations and media in [media and visual support](media-and-visual-support.md).

## Distribute a lesson

A lesson is a folder: `lesson.json`, its `assets/` and, once approved, `approval.json`. Keep the three together and at the same revision. A lesson shipped as a `.zip` carries the record as its member `approval.json` (the demo build scripts add it when it matches `lesson.json`); without it the lesson reads "No approval is recorded for this lesson." Students place the folder in their Studium library (by default `~/.studium/library/<course_id>/`, or the folder `BUNDLES_ROOT` names) and open it from their assistant or from VS Code (see [VS Code](../start/vscode.md)). When a learner starts the lesson, the session reports whether an approval record matches the exact file.

For a class:

- start with a few students and check the session on their machines (bundle access, display, language, behaviour when the model or the network is unavailable, export); - give written instructions and a fallback if the assistant account or the internet fails; - the VS Code package makes the lesson pane easy to install, but it does not distribute or validate lessons for you.

## Run an experiment session

When a lesson lets students explore with their assistant, set a concrete scope: data, commands, dependencies, web access, interactive controls and duration. Redisplaying the approved materials can stay inside the activity; a new claim, exercise or scene generated beyond that scope is a draft you review before use. Studium does not yet enforce that boundary for you.

Ask students for their prediction, the differences they observed, one limit and a transfer test. An agent's output is not evidence that the student understood. The [agentic experiment tutorial](../tutorials/agentic-experiment.md) gives a full run, and [literature and evidence](literature-and-evidence.md) explains the portable exploration receipt.

## What students can share with you

A student may choose to export a [learner report](../learn/learner-report.md) of their recorded actions, and keeps a private [experiment journal](../learn/experiment-journal.md). Discuss with them what will be shared and how you will read it: an incomplete trace does not measure autonomy. The default report excludes personal text and gives no access to the full journal or the assistant's history. See [privacy and limits](../concepts/privacy-and-limits.md).

The [interaction report](follow-a-class.md#how-the-interface-was-used) shows how a consenting class used the interface. To lay those class figures over the lesson's concepts, use `tools/concept_map_report.py` and the [concept map's teacher viewpoint](../learn/concept-map.md#the-teacher-viewpoint-and-class-figures).

## Limits

- Technical checks (schema, exact quotes, lint) are not a pedagogical review; an exact quote can still be misread. - The approval record names the reviewer you type; Studium does not authenticate it. - The dashboard, Observatory and analytics services are local tools without login; do not expose them on the internet.
